plan: Ten new items plus S029-03 resubmitted (monarch distance reworded). Topics checked against bank titles; WIC keys (tacit, belied) checked against the bank's existing WIC answers: tacit/belied WIC, coyote-diet inference, window-treatment percent-change data, dog-pointing cross-text, mantis-shrimp synthesis, otters 'Even so,', appositive comma, past-perfect verb, Draupner sentence function. (Long-subject agreement and an overall-structure item were dropped at screening as repeats of bank items 091/035 and 235.)

passages.title: Prices without minutes
passages.text: No rule in the guild's charter forbade members from undercutting one another's prices, yet historians believe members observed a ______ understanding on the matter: the records of guild meetings never mention prices at all, but members' prices stayed within a few pennies of one another for decades.

passages.title: A small jaw
passages.text: The fossil's modest size ______ its significance: the jaw, barely two centimeters long, preserves a pattern of tooth replacement that researchers had predicted for fish of its age but had never before observed.

passages.title: A relay across generations
passages.text: Each fall, monarch butterflies from eastern North America fly thousands of kilometers to forests in central Mexico, where they spend the winter. In spring they head north, but no individual completes the return. The butterflies breed along the way, and it is their children and grandchildren that continue the journey and reach the northern United States and Canada. The monarchs that fly south again in the fall may therefore be the great-grandchildren of those that left Mexico in spring.

passages.title: Urban coyotes
passages.text: Food from people, such as garbage and pet food, is plentiful in cities and takes little effort for coyotes to obtain, so one might expect urban coyotes that eat it to be healthier than coyotes that hunt. A 2015 study in Edmonton, Canada, found the reverse: coyotes whose diets included more human food were in poorer body condition and more likely to have mange. One possible explanation is that human food, though plentiful, is low in the protein that coyotes need, which would mean that ______

passages.title: Window treatments
passages.text:
Researchers recorded the average number of bird collisions per month at office buildings before and after one of three window treatments was installed.
Treatment | Before | After
Dot-pattern film | 20 | 6
UV-reflective glass | 40 | 22
Exterior netting | 10 | 4
The researchers concluded that, relative to each building group's starting level, the dot-pattern film was the most effective of the three treatments.

passages.title: Following a point (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
In experiments where a person points to one of two cups hiding food, pet dogs choose the correct cup far more often than chimpanzees do. Some researchers have concluded that domestication gave dogs an inborn sensitivity to human gestures that their wild relatives lack.
Text 2
Other researchers have found that wolves raised by people from birth can follow pointing about as well as pet dogs, while shelter dogs with little human contact often struggle with the task. These researchers argue that a dog's experience with people shapes this skill more than has been recognized.

passages.title: Twelve receptors
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Humans have three types of color photoreceptors.
• Mantis shrimp have twelve types of color photoreceptors.
• Researchers expected mantis shrimp to tell apart very similar colors.
• In a 2014 study, mantis shrimp could not reliably distinguish colors that people can easily tell apart.
• The researchers suggested that the shrimp may identify colors directly instead of comparing signals from different receptors.

passages.title: Otters and kelp
passages.text: Sea otters eat sea urchins, and where otters have returned to the coast, urchin numbers have dropped and kelp forests have regrown. ______ the otters' appetite for shellfish has brought them into conflict with people who harvest crabs and clams.

passages.title: An unread manuscript
passages.text: The Voynich manuscript, a fifteenth-century book written in an unknown ______ has resisted every attempt at decipherment, including efforts by professional codebreakers during the twentieth century.

passages.title: A contaminated plate
passages.text: In September 1928, Alexander Fleming returned from a vacation and found that a mold had contaminated one of the culture plates in his laboratory. He noticed that the mold growing on the plate ______ the bacteria immediately around it.

passages.title: Draupner wave
passages.text: For decades, sailors' reports of "rogue waves" (single waves more than twice as tall as the surrounding seas) were often dismissed as exaggerations, since standard models predicted that such waves should be extremely rare. Then, on January 1, 1995, a laser sensor on the Draupner oil platform in the North Sea recorded a wave about 26 meters high amid seas of roughly 12 meters. Researchers have since revised their models, and satellite surveys suggest rogue waves are more common than once believed.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: the records of guild meetings never mention prices at all
candidates.explanation: The understanding was never recorded yet was consistently followed for decades, so it was unspoken but shared: "tacit."

A.rationale: A formal understanding would likely appear in the meeting records, which never mention prices.

B.rationale: Prices that stayed close together for decades suggest a stable understanding, not a fragile one.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests disagreement; the evidence shows quiet, consistent agreement.

candidates.remember: Use both halves of the evidence: what is missing and what still happened.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: barely two centimeters long, preserves a pattern
candidates.explanation: A tiny fossil turns out to be very important, so its size gave a false impression of its significance: it "belied" it.

B.rationale: Its small size did not reflect its importance; the colon introduces how important it is despite being tiny.

C.rationale: A small size would understate, not exaggerate, the fossil's importance.

D.rationale: The fossil's size did not cause its significance; the tooth pattern did.

hints: Does the size match the importance, or hide it?
candidates.remember: A contrast between appearance and reality points to words like "belied" or "masked."

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Monarch butterflies spend the winter in forests in central Mexico.
choices.B: Monarchs fly farther each spring than they do each fall.
choices.C: Most monarch butterflies die before they reach central Mexico in the fall.
choices.D: No single monarch completes the yearly round trip; several generations do.

candidates.explanation: The text's focus is that the migration is a relay: the northbound trip is completed by later generations, and the fall migrants may be great-grandchildren of the spring migrants.

A.rationale: This is a detail from the first sentence, not the main idea.

B.rationale: The text does not compare the distances of the two journeys.

C.rationale: The text says nothing about how many monarchs fail to reach Mexico.

hints: What is surprising about who makes the return trip?

strategy.explanation: Summarize the text in one sentence.

candidates.remember: A main idea covers the whole text, not its opening detail.

revision_history.change: Replaced 'as far as 4,000 kilometers', which understates the eastern migration, with 'thousands of kilometers'; key letter moved from A to D. Item otherwise unchanged and re-solved blind.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: coyotes that hunt spend less effort finding food than coyotes that eat human food.
choices.B: how easy a food is to obtain can matter less to a coyote's health than what the food contains.
choices.C: coyotes would stop eating human food if they could find enough wild prey.
choices.D: mange in urban coyotes is caused mainly by eating too much protein.

candidates.evidence: low in the protein that coyotes need
candidates.explanation: The text expects easy food to mean better health, then explains the opposite result by the food's poor protein content. So ease of getting food matters less than its nutritional content.

A.rationale: The text says human food takes little effort to obtain, so this reverses it.

C.rationale: The text says nothing about what coyotes would choose to eat.

D.rationale: The explanation is that human food is low in protein, the opposite of too much.

hints: What did people expect, and what explains the actual result?

strategy.explanation: State the contrast between ease and nutrition.

candidates.remember: An inference completion must follow from the explanation the text offers.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers' conclusion?

choices.A: Collisions fell by 18 per month with UV-reflective glass, the largest drop of the three.
choices.B: Buildings with netting had the fewest collisions both before and after treatment.
choices.C: Buildings with dot-pattern film had fewer collisions afterward than those with UV glass.
choices.D: Collisions fell by 70% with dot-pattern film, 45% with UV glass, and 60% with netting.

candidates.evidence: relative to each building group's starting level
candidates.explanation: Relative reductions: dot film (20-6)/20 = 70%, UV glass (40-22)/40 = 45%, netting (10-4)/10 = 60%. The dot film's 70% is the largest, supporting the conclusion.

A.rationale: This is the largest drop in number, but the conclusion is about change relative to each starting level, and it favors UV glass.

B.rationale: This is true but does not compare how much each treatment reduced collisions relative to its start.

C.rationale: Comparing final counts ignores the different starting levels, which the conclusion explicitly accounts for.

hints: Is the conclusion about the size of the drop or the percentage?
candidates.remember: "Relative to the starting level" means percent change, not raw change.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion described in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing with it, since wolves' performance shows that the skill is inherited
choices.B: By arguing that chimpanzees would follow pointing as well as dogs if they were tested by familiar people
choices.C: By arguing that it overlooks how much contact with people during development contributes to the skill
choices.D: By claiming that pet dogs are actually worse than shelter dogs at following human gestures

candidates.evidence: a dog's experience with people shapes this skill more than has been recognized
candidates.explanation: Text 1 credits an inborn trait from domestication; Text 2's evidence (human-raised wolves succeed, shelter dogs struggle) points to experience with people, so Text 2 would say Text 1 overlooks that factor.

A.rationale: Human-raised wolves succeeding suggests experience, not domestication, matters, which challenges Text 1.

B.rationale: Text 2 says nothing about chimpanzees or who did the testing.

D.rationale: Text 2 says shelter dogs often struggle, the opposite of this claim.

hints: What does each group think explains the skill?

strategy.explanation: Name each text's explanation before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: In cross-text items, find exactly where the second view disagrees.

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize the surprising result of the 2014 study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Despite having four times as many types of color photoreceptors as humans, mantis shrimp were worse at telling similar colors apart.
choices.B: Mantis shrimp have twelve types of color photoreceptors, while humans have only three types of these photoreceptors.
choices.C: In a 2014 study, researchers tested how well mantis shrimp, which have twelve receptor types, could distinguish colors.
choices.D: Researchers have suggested that mantis shrimp may identify colors directly rather than by comparing receptor signals.

candidates.evidence: could not reliably distinguish colors that people can easily tell apart
candidates.explanation: The surprise is the contrast between the expectation (more receptors, finer color vision) and the result (worse discrimination than humans). Only A states both parts; twelve is four times three.

B.rationale: This states the difference in receptors but not the study's surprising result.

C.rationale: This describes the study's purpose without stating its surprising result.

D.rationale: This gives the researchers' explanation, not the surprising result itself.

hints: What did researchers expect, and what happened?

strategy.explanation: Read the goal first, then look for the choice that pairs expectation with result.

candidates.remember: Emphasizing a surprise means stating both the expectation and the result that defied it.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.explanation: The first sentence describes a benefit of otters' return; the second introduces a drawback despite that benefit, so a concessive transition, "Even so," fits.

A.rationale: The conflict with fishers is a drawback, not a further benefit like the kelp's recovery.

C.rationale: The kelp's regrowth does not cause the conflict with shellfish harvesters.

D.rationale: The second sentence adds a new problem; it does not restate the first.

hints: Is the second sentence good news or bad news about otters?
candidates.remember: Benefit followed by drawback calls for a contrast or concession.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: The Voynich manuscript, a fifteenth-century book
candidates.explanation: The phrase "a fifteenth-century book written in an unknown script" interrupts the subject and verb and began with a comma, so it must close with a comma.

A.rationale: Without a comma, the appositive that began after "manuscript," is never closed.

B.rationale: An appositive that opens with a comma cannot close with a dash.

D.rationale: A semicolon would separate the subject from its verb, "has resisted."

hints: Where does the phrase describing the manuscript begin, and how?

strategy.explanation: Match the punctuation that opens the phrase.

candidates.remember: Paired punctuation must match: comma with comma, dash with dash.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: He noticed that the mold growing on the plate
candidates.explanation: The clause after "that" needs a finite verb, and the killing happened before Fleming noticed it in the past, so the past perfect "had killed" is correct.

B.rationale: The present perfect does not fit a narrative set in 1928; the killing happened before Fleming noticed it.

C.rationale: Without a finite verb, the clause after "that" has no main verb.

D.rationale: An infinitive leaves the clause after "that" without a main verb.

hints: Which choice gives the clause a verb that fits a past-tense narrative?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that leave the clause without a main verb.

candidates.remember: An action completed before another past action takes the past perfect ("had" + past participle).

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It offers an example of the kind of exaggerated report that the models were designed to explain.
choices.B: It explains how researchers revised their models so that they could predict the Draupner wave.
choices.C: It provides evidence that rogue waves are more common today than they were in earlier decades.
choices.D: It reports a direct observation that was difficult to reconcile with the models mentioned earlier.

candidates.evidence: recorded a wave about 26 meters high amid seas of roughly 12 meters
candidates.explanation: The first sentence says models predicted rogue waves (over twice the surrounding sea height) to be extremely rare; the second reports an instrument measuring a 26-meter wave amid 12-meter seas, a direct observation at odds with those models.

A.rationale: The 1995 record was an instrument measurement, not a sailor's exaggeration, and it contradicted the models.

B.rationale: The revision is mentioned only in the third sentence, as a later consequence.

C.rationale: The text says rogue waves are more common than once believed, not that they have become more frequent.

hints: Is the 1995 wave a sailor's report or a measurement?

strategy.explanation: Describe what the sentence does relative to the first sentence.

candidates.remember: A function question asks what a sentence does, not just what it says.
